slot.brief: Using the Rydberg relation, ask for the ratio or value of wavelength/energy for a transition in Lyman or Balmer, e.g. compare the n=2→1 and n=3→2 lines via 1/λ scaling; harder reasoning, so make the algebra slightly involved.

stem: If the wavelength of the first line of the Lyman series in the hydrogen atom spectrum is $\lambda$, the difference between the longest and shortest wavelengths of the Balmer series is

verdicts.working: Lyman first line: 1/λ = R(1−1/4) = 3R/4 ⇒ λ = 4/(3R). Balmer longest (3→2): λ_L = 36/(5R); shortest (∞→2): λ_S = 4/R. Difference = 16/(5R) = (16/5)(3λ/4) = 12λ/5.

working:
According to the Rydberg formula for hydrogen ($Z = 1$):
$$\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_\text{H} \left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$$

1. For the first line of the Lyman series ($n_1 = 1$, $n_2 = 2$):
$$\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_\text{H}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{4}\right) = \dfrac{3}{4}R_\text{H} \implies \dfrac{1}{R_\text{H}} = \dfrac{3}{4}\lambda$$

2. For the Balmer series ($n_1 = 2$):
- The longest wavelength ($\lambda_{\max}$) corresponds to the transition with minimum energy ($n_2 = 3$):
$$\dfrac{1}{\lambda_{\max}} = R_\text{H}\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{9}\right) = \dfrac{5}{36}R_\text{H} \implies \lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{36}{5R_\text{H}}$$

- The shortest wavelength ($\lambda_{\min}$) corresponds to the series limit ($n_2 = \infty$):
$$\dfrac{1}{\lambda_{\min}} = R_\text{H}\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - 0\right) = \dfrac{R_\text{H}}{4} \implies \lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{4}{R_\text{H}}$$

3. The difference in wavelength is:
$$\Delta \lambda = \lambda_{\max} - \lambda_{\min} = \left(\dfrac{36}{5} - 4\right)\dfrac{1}{R_\text{H}} = \dfrac{16}{5R_\text{H}}$$

Substitute $\dfrac{1}{R_\text{H}} = \dfrac{3}{4}\lambda$:
$$\Delta \lambda = \dfrac{16}{5} \times \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\lambda\right) = \dfrac{12}{5}\lambda$$

Independent check: Lyman first line: 1/λ = R(1−1/4) = 3R/4 ⇒ λ = 4/(3R). Balmer longest (3→2): λ_L = 36/(5R); shortest (∞→2): λ_S = 4/R. Difference = 16/(5R) = (16/5)(3λ/4) = 12λ/5.

draft.distractor_notes:
$\dfrac{7}{5}\lambda$: Mistakenly considers the shortest wavelength of Balmer as the second line ($n = 4 \rightarrow 2$) rather than the series limit ($n = \infty \rightarrow 2$), giving $\left(\dfrac{36}{5} - \dfrac{16}{3}\right)\dfrac{3\lambda}{4} = \dfrac{7}{5}\lambda$.
$\dfrac{8}{5}\lambda$: Forgets to square the principal quantum numbers in the Lyman transition, using $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_\text{H}(1 - 1/2) = \dfrac{R_\text{H}}{2} \implies \dfrac{1}{R_\text{H}} = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$, giving $\dfrac{16}{5} \times \dfrac{\lambda}{2} = \dfrac{8}{5}\lambda$.
$\dfrac{16}{5}\lambda$: Forgets the factor of $3/4$ from the first Lyman line relation (effectively assuming $\lambda$ is the Lyman series limit where $R_\text{H} = 1/\lambda$).
